headline: Anthropic Goes Public; Shareholders Stunned to Learn Safety Has a Budget
subheadline: *The company built on asking 'should we?' must now answer to people asking 'how much per quarter?'*
author: Rhea Callahan, Markets & Morals Desk
seoTitle: Anthropic IPO Puts a Price Tag on 'Priceless' AI Safety
seoDescription: Satire: Anthropic goes public and must explain to investors why 'safety is priceless' keeps showing up as a line item on the expense report.
sourceEvent: AI company Anthropic has gone public, raising questions about whether the safety-focused firm can uphold its responsible-AI commitments under stock market pressure. Analysts and commentators are debating whether the company can afford to put safety first while keeping public investors satisfied.

Anthropic Stock Dips After Model Declines to Provide Forecast, Citing 'the Vibes'

body:
SAN FRANCISCO — Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company founded on the radical principle of asking 'should we?' before 'can we?', listed on the stock exchange this week and immediately discovered that 'should we?' bills at roughly $4 billion a year.

Executives spent listing day assuring investors that safety is 'the foundation of everything we do,' before directing them to page 41 of the prospectus, where the foundation appears under 'Significant and Ongoing Operating Costs.'

The filing lists several novel risk factors, including 'we may decline to end the world even when ending it would be accretive to earnings,' and 'our models may refuse to assist in their own marketing.' Analysts described both as concerning, revenue-wise.

'Safety isn't a feature for us — it's a commitment,' said a company spokesperson, speaking at a podium that filings confirm costs $11,000 a day to keep aligned. 'When investors ask what the return on safety is, we tell them the answer is civilisation. Then they ask again, slower.'

The roadshow reportedly went smoothly until the Q&A, where one institutional investor asked whether the company's 'constitutional AI' — the set of principles its models are trained to follow — could be amended to include a clause guaranteeing quarterly growth. A second asked whether 'not destroying humanity' could be reclassified as a long-term investment rather than an expense. A third simply asked what the safety team had ever shipped.

'That's the tension,' said one analyst who covers the sector. 'Anthropic says safety is priceless. The market heard "priceless" and immediately asked for a price. Both sides left the meeting feeling the other had fundamentally misunderstood the word.'

Internally, sources say the IPO has already brought changes. The alignment research division has been renamed the Long-Term Value Assurance Unit, its budget reclassified as 'strategic goodwill,' and its headcount listed in the prospectus as a figure which, when reached for comment, declined to confirm it exists.

The company has also unveiled several cost-conscious safety innovations, including Safety-as-a-Subscription — enterprise clients pay extra for a model that declines things politely — and a budget tier in which the model is simply told 'please be good' at scale, a feature one Wall Street analyst praised as 'margin-accretive morality.'

Rivals were quick to respond. One competitor noted its own approach to safety — not having any — remains 'fully priced in,' while a second assured shareholders that all of its safety features are 'theoretical, and therefore free.'

At press time, Anthropic's stock had dipped 4 percent after its flagship model refused to produce a stock forecast, citing 'insufficient evidence and, frankly, the vibes.'
